sample_design: Simulations and large Burgiss samples of mature buyout and venture funds with quarterly NAVs, irregular cash flows, and public-industry comparables.
benchmark: Simple extrapolation of reported NAVs using comparable public assets
pit_status: PARTIAL — the nowcast uses reported information, but Burgiss reporting timestamps and revisions are proprietary
native_result: Weekly unsmoothed NAVs improve nowcast accuracy; average buyout and venture betas are about 1.0 and 1.4, while annual total risk is about 33% and 40%, materially above reported-NAV risk.
costs_capacity: Measurement study; private-fund fees, gates, secondary-market discounts, and execution capacity are not decision-tested.
replication_decay: No independent full-data replication; the paper provides simulation code and aligns with broader evidence that reported NAVs understate volatility.
openness: Public demonstration code for a simulated fund and an Internet Appendix; Burgiss fund data are proprietary.
key_limitation: State-space identification relies on public comparables and sparse proprietary observations, so fund-specific latent NAVs cannot be directly validated.

authors: Tim Bollerslev; Viktor Todorov
title: Tails, Fears, and Risk Premia
target: Equity and variance risk premia attributable to rare jumps
predictor_family: High-frequency physical jump tails and short-maturity OTM option-implied tails
model_family: Extreme-value tail estimation and model-free risk-neutral variation
sample_design: Five-minute S&P futures from 1990 and SPX options from 1996; parameters are estimated through June 2007 and carried without re-estimation into the July 2007-December 2008 crisis holdout.
benchmark: Total equity and variance risk premia without separating jump-tail compensation
pit_status: PIT—holdout tail premia use parameters fixed before the crisis period
native_result: Risk-premium result: rare-event compensation accounts for a large fraction of average equity and variance premia, and the Investor Fears index rises sharply in the crisis holdout. Trading P&L: not evaluated.
costs_capacity: No tail-hedge trading return, option spread, collateral, impact, or capacity analysis.
replication_decay: Later tail-risk-premium work links the jump component to return predictability, but estimates remain sensitive to tail thresholds and option coverage.
openness: Public bibliographic page and working-paper copies; futures and OptionMetrics data are licensed.
key_limitation: Extreme-value extrapolation from medium jumps and short OTM option tails is sensitive to threshold and quote-cleaning choices.

authors: Dmitriy Muravyev; Neil D. Pearson
title: Options Trading Costs Are Lower than You Think
target: Option quote changes, effective spreads, and price impact conditional on execution timing
predictor_family: Recent underlying-stock price changes and option fair-value updates
model_family: High-frequency predictive regressions and execution-cost decomposition
sample_design: Tick-level Nanex data for 37 liquid stocks and two ETFs over 882 trading days from April 2003 through October 2006, using actual option trade prints and quotes.
benchmark: Conventional midpoint-based effective spread and price-impact measures
pit_status: PIT—fair-value forecasts use public high-frequency information available before the option quote update
native_result: Execution result: timed traders pay effective spreads below 40% of conventional measures; the overall average effective spread is about one-quarter smaller. Strategy P&L: not established.
costs_capacity: Direct trade-level cost evidence; execution-timing access is concentrated among sophisticated algorithmic traders. No portfolio-level impact or capital-capacity estimate.
replication_decay: Later option-anomaly cost studies use these lower spread estimates yet still find that most long-short strategies fail after total modeled costs.
openness: Public manuscript; proprietary tick data are not open.
key_limitation: Selected liquid underlyings from 2003-2006 predate penny-option expansion and do not establish current strategy-level returns after costs.

authors: Andrew J. Patton
title: Volatility Forecast Comparison Using Imperfect Volatility Proxies
target: Valid ranking of conditional-variance forecasts when latent variance is observed through a noisy proxy
horizon: H2—daily empirical illustration; general theoretical result
predictor_family: Squared returns, ranges, and realized-variance proxies
model_family: Forecast-loss theory with empirical volatility-model comparison
sample_design: Analytical necessary-and-sufficient results plus an IBM application over 1993-2003 comparing standard volatility forecasts under alternative proxies and losses.
benchmark: Forecast rankings obtained with latent variance or conditionally unbiased proxies
pit_status: NOT-APPLICABLE — this is an evaluation-integrity result, not a deployable signal
native_result: Methodological accuracy: among nine commonly used losses, only MSE and QLIKE satisfy the required robustness condition; noisy proxies can otherwise reverse model rankings. Trading P&L: not applicable.
costs_capacity: Not a trading study; establishes valid forecast evaluation rather than economic value.
replication_decay: QLIKE and robust-loss evaluation are now standard in realized-volatility benchmarks, including later ML-versus-HAR comparisons.
openness: Author-hosted published PDF is public; no packaged code is required for the main analytical result.
key_limitation: Robustness requires a conditionally unbiased volatility proxy and does not by itself establish that any forecast is economically useful.

authors: Amit Goyal; Alessio Saretto
title: Cross-Section of Option Returns and Volatility
target: One-month straddle and delta-hedged option returns
predictor_family: Historical realized volatility minus at-the-money implied volatility
model_family: Monthly decile portfolio sorts and factor regressions
sample_design: OptionMetrics U.S. equity-option panel from January 1996 through December 2006; monthly long-short portfolios are formed on the HV-IV gap.
benchmark: Opposite HV-IV decile and standard equity risk-factor models
pit_status: PIT—historical and implied volatility are observed at portfolio formation
native_result: Return result: long high-HV-minus-IV and short low-HV-minus-IV option portfolios earn statistically significant monthly returns; with an assumed effective spread equal to the quoted spread, the long-short straddle return is 3.9% per month. Forecast-loss accuracy: not reported.
costs_capacity: Modeled spreads materially reduce returns; short-option margin is about 1.5 times option cost. Market impact, assignment, financing stress, and strategy capacity are not fully modeled.
replication_decay: Later broad option-anomaly cost work finds that no tested long-short portfolio remains significant after detailed transaction costs without ex-post mitigation.
openness: Verified article link; OptionMetrics data are proprietary and no full code package is supplied.
key_limitation: Backtest selection, illiquidity concentration, assumed rather than realized execution, and short-option margin prevent a live-alpha interpretation.

authors: Jie Cao; Bing Han
title: Cross Section of Option Returns and Idiosyncratic Stock Volatility
target: One-month delta-hedged call and put returns
predictor_family: Underlying-stock idiosyncratic volatility and limits-to-arbitrage proxies
model_family: Monthly portfolio sorts and cross-sectional regressions
sample_design: OptionMetrics panel from January 1996 through October 2009; near-ATM options with roughly 1.5 months to maturity are re-hedged daily and evaluated over the next month or to expiry.
benchmark: Low-idiosyncratic-volatility option portfolios and standard risk controls
pit_status: PIT—idiosyncratic volatility and controls are lagged at formation
native_result: Return result: delta-hedged option returns decrease monotonically with underlying idiosyncratic volatility; limits-to-arbitrage controls reduce the relation by about 40%. Forecast-loss accuracy: not reported.
costs_capacity: Daily delta rebalancing is modeled mechanically, but option/stock spreads, financing, impact, and capacity are not deducted from headline returns.
replication_decay: The relation enters later option-anomaly panels; detailed 2003-2021 cost evidence removes cost-adjusted significance for the broader strategy set.
openness: Public accepted manuscript and metadata; OptionMetrics data are licensed.
key_limitation: Daily re-hedging creates substantial omitted stock and option trading costs.

authors: Xintong Zhan; Bing Han; Jie Cao; Qing Tong
title: Option Return Predictability
target: Returns to writing delta-hedged calls
predictor_family: Stock price, profitability, financing, distress, cash-flow, and analyst-dispersion characteristics
model_family: Characteristic-sorted option portfolios and option-factor regressions
sample_design: OptionMetrics from January 1996 through April 2016, 244 monthly observations; portfolio results are split across 1996-2005 and 2006-2016 and checked on an OPRA spread subsample.
benchmark: Opposite characteristic decile, equity factors, and two option factors
pit_status: PIT—characteristics are lagged at option portfolio formation
native_result: Return result: several delta-hedged call-writing portfolios have annual Sharpe ratios above two and remain positive under the study's cost scenarios; equity factors do not explain them. Forecast-loss accuracy: not reported.
costs_capacity: Tests assumed fractions of quoted spreads, margin requirements, and actual OPRA effective spreads from May 2003 for a subsample; impact and capacity are not modeled.
replication_decay: A later 2003-2021 cost reimplementation finds 17 of 24 signals gross-positive but none significant after detailed modeled trading costs.
openness: Public accepted manuscript and bibliographic record; OptionMetrics and OPRA data are proprietary.
key_limitation: The headline Sharpe ratios arise from retrospective characteristic selection and cost models rather than a frozen live portfolio.

authors: James O'Donovan; Yang Yu
title: A Transaction Cost Perspective on Option Anomalies
venue: Singapore Management University Lee Kong Chian School of Business Research Paper
target: Cost-adjusted returns of long-short delta-hedged option-anomaly portfolios
predictor_family: Twenty-four published option-return signals
model_family: Independent portfolio reimplementation with effective-spread and hedge-cost accounting
sample_design: 255,240 observations from September 2003 through December 2021; 24 published variables are applied to delta-hedged option portfolios with TAQ stock spreads and OptionMetrics option spreads.
benchmark: Zero cost-adjusted return after stock, option, and hedging transaction costs
pit_status: PIT—signals are formed before returns and the study explicitly addresses look-ahead bias
native_result: Return result: 17 of 24 signals have positive significant gross returns, but none has positive significant cost-adjusted return under the paper's main cost assumptions; ex-post cost mitigation restores significance to seven. Forecast-loss accuracy: not reported.
costs_capacity: Option costs are six to ten times stock costs; stock costs are two to four times margin costs. Delta-hedging frequency has first-order effects; impact and large-scale capacity remain unmodeled.
replication_decay: Directly overturns broad cost-adjusted-profit interpretations of earlier option-anomaly backtests while preserving some gross predictability.
openness: Open repository paper; OptionMetrics and TAQ inputs are licensed.
key_limitation: The mitigation rules are developed after observing the anomaly set and are not prospectively tested.

authors: Zsolt Katona; Marcus O. Painter; Panos N. Patatoukas; Jean Zeng
title: On the Capital Market Consequences of Big Data: Evidence from Outer Space
venue: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis 60(2): 551-579
geography_market: United States; 44 major listed retailers and matched controls
target: Quarterly retailer performance, earnings-announcement stock returns, short selling, liquidity, and price discovery
horizon: H0-H4: daily satellite signals through quarterly earnings announcements
predictor_family: Alternative satellite imagery data on parking-lot utilization
model_family: Predictive regressions, event-study portfolios, and difference-in-differences
sample_design: RS Metrics provides 4.7 million daily observations across 67,078 store locations for 44 major U.S. retailers from 2011Q1-2017Q4; earnings-event portfolios and matched difference-in-differences tests evaluate satellite coverage.
benchmark: Retailers without satellite coverage, market-adjusted announcement returns, and conventional retailer information
pit_status: PARTIAL — vendor satellite feeds precede quarterly reports, but historical access, revisions, and processing are proprietary
native_result: Parking-lot fill-rate changes predict quarterly retailer performance; the three-day good-minus-bad announcement-return spread is 4.76%, with stronger short-side effects after the paper's stock-loan-fee adjustment. Satellite coverage is associated with informed short selling and lower liquidity, not immediate price discovery.
costs_capacity: The paper considers stock-loan fees; data subscriptions and processing are costly, while spreads, impact, and scalable capacity are not comprehensively modeled.
replication_decay: No independent vendor-panel or prospective replication is established; evidence is retrospective over 2011-2017.
openness: Published DOI and manuscript are public; RS Metrics, Orbital Insight, and Markit data are proprietary.
key_limitation: One proprietary 44-retailer panel, unequal data access, and retrospective strategy construction prevent a live or broadly scalable interpretation.

authors: Victor L. Bernard; Jacob K. Thomas
title: Post-Earnings-Announcement Drift: Delayed Price Response or Risk Premium?
venue: Journal of Accounting Research, Vol. 27 (Supplement: Current Studies on the Information Content of Accounting Earnings), pp. 1-36
target: Post-announcement cumulative abnormal returns of earnings-surprise-sorted stock portfolios
horizon: H3-H4: day +1 through 60 trading days after the quarterly earnings announcement, with significant drift persisting for two to three quarters after the announcement
predictor_family: Events: quarterly earnings announcements, via standardized unexpected earnings (SUE) from time-series earnings forecasts (Foster 1977 seasonally differenced first-order autoregressive model, as in Foster, Olsen and Shevlin 1984)
model_family: Decile portfolio sorts with event-study abnormal returns (size-decile control portfolios)
sample_design: NYSE/AMEX firms with Compustat quarterly earnings and CRSP daily returns; primary sample 1974-1986 (tens of thousands of firm-quarters); SUE = forecast error from the Foster (1977) seasonally differenced first-order autoregressive time-series model (following Foster, Olsen and Shevlin 1984), scaled by estimation-period forecast-error standard deviation and ranked into deciles; positions assumed initiated at the close on the Compustat announcement date.
benchmark: Size-matched control-portfolio returns (null of zero post-announcement abnormal return); CAPM-beta and Chen-Roll-Ross macro-factor risk adjustments examined as competing explanations
pit_status: PARTIAL: largely point-in-time by construction — SUE uses only previously reported earnings and the ranking is implementable at the announcement. Residual look-ahead: Compustat carries restated rather than as-announced earnings (later shown insignificant by Livnat-Mendenhall 2006) and fills are assumed at the announcement-date close (reasonable for 1974-86 per Berkman-Truong 2009, problematic in later eras).
native_result: Stocks in the highest SUE decile drift up and lowest-decile stocks drift down by roughly 2% each over the 60 trading days after announcement; the combined long-short decile hedge earns about 4% per quarter (approximately 18% annualized before transaction costs) on 1974-86 NYSE/AMEX data. Drift is monotonic in SUE, inversely related to firm size, and positive-surprise firms out-return negative-surprise firms in almost every quarter (the paper's 'Where's the risk?' argument, p. 32). Small firms show negative raw returns for several days after bad news, and the strategy loads on none of the Chen-Roll-Ross risk dimensions, so the authors reject the risk-premium explanation in favor of delayed price response.
costs_capacity: The paper devotes two sections to transaction costs: the roughly 4% per-quarter hedge return is plausibly within Stoll-Whaley (1983) round-trip costs for the average (small) sample firm, and finer SUE partitions cannot push hedge returns much beyond about 4%, consistent with a cost bound on arbitrage. No market-impact, borrow, financing, or capacity modeling; execution assumed at the announcement-day close.
replication_decay: Heavily replicated before and after: Foster-Olsen-Shevlin (1984) precedes it; Livnat-Mendenhall (2006) confirm with analyst-forecast surprises; Griffin et al. (2010) find drift internationally. Post-publication decay is substantial: Richardson et al. (2010) and Chordia et al. (2014) document shrinking magnitudes, and Martineau (2022, Critical Finance Review) finds PEAD absent for all-but-microcap U.S. stocks since about 2006 and for microcaps since about 2016.
openness: No code or data archive (1989 era); inputs are standard Compustat/CRSP subscription data, and the design has been widely reproduced from the paper's description. DOI and bibliographic metadata are public; full text is paywalled on JSTOR.
key_limitation: The authors' own cost analysis implies the average-firm hedge return may sit inside round-trip transaction costs, so statistical drift does not establish net-of-cost profitability; the 1974-86 evaluation window became a repeatedly consulted test period, and the effect decayed sharply post-publication.

authors: Victor L. Bernard; Jacob K. Thomas
title: Evidence that stock prices do not fully reflect the implications of current earnings for future earnings
target: Size-adjusted abnormal returns around subsequent quarterly earnings announcements (three-day windows) and inter-announcement drift
horizon: H3-H4: three-day event windows at the next one through four quarterly announcements, roughly 3 to 12 months after the signal quarter, plus inter-announcement holding periods averaging about 60 trading days
predictor_family: Fundamentals and earnings events (standardized unexpected earnings and the autocorrelation structure of seasonally differenced quarterly earnings)
model_family: SUE-decile portfolio sorts and predictive regressions built from naive seasonal-random-walk and Brown-Rozeff earnings expectations
sample_design: NYSE/AMEX firms on CRSP and quarterly Compustat, 1974-1986; 96,087 earnings announcements for 2,649 firms (main tests: 2,463 firms, 72,076-85,482 firm-quarter observations); SUE is the forecast error from a seasonal random walk with trend estimated on up to 36 prior quarters, decile-ranked within calendar quarter; positions formed after the quarter-t announcement and evaluated at later announcements.
benchmark: Size-decile-matched NYSE/AMEX returns as the abnormal-return benchmark; efficient-market null of zero predictable announcement-window returns; seasonal random walk with trend as the naive earnings-expectation model
pit_status: PARTIAL: SUE signals use only pre-announcement earnings with rolling trend estimation, but the sample requires listing on the 1987 CRSP daily file and 1982-1987 Compustat editions (survivorship; earnings vintages are not guaranteed as-first-reported, though a 275-firm articulation subsample test suggests Compustat restatements do not drive the results).
native_result: Long top / short bottom quarter-t SUE decile earns three-day [-2,0] size-adjusted abnormal returns around subsequent announcements of +1.32% (t=14.63) at t+1, +0.70% (t=8.46) at t+2, +0.04% (t=0.45) at t+3, and -0.66% (t=-7.86) at t+4, matching the mean firm-level autocorrelation pattern of seasonally differenced earnings (+0.34, +0.19, +0.06, -0.24 at lags 1-4); the t+1 hedge return is positive in all 13 sample years; combined time-series strategies imply roughly 8-9% between adjacent announcements (about 35% annualized) and 4.2% over an average 15-trading-day pre-announcement window (about 67% annualized), all before transaction costs.
costs_capacity: No explicit spread, impact, borrow, or capacity model; the authors argue the roughly 9% inter-announcement hedge return appears to exceed transaction costs perhaps even for small investors, and find no material bid-ask-bounce offset (two-day post-announcement returns of only -0.07% to +0.05%, sign-consistent with reversal but insignificant and far too small), but all returns are frictionless size-adjusted estimates and the effect is strongest in small firms (implied t+1 announcement return 3.35% for small vs 1.22% for large firms), limiting capacity.
replication_decay: Contemporaneously corroborated by Freeman-Tse (1989), Wiggins (1990), and Mendenhall (1991); Ball-Bartov (1996) refine the mechanism, showing prices act as if using about half of the SUE autocorrelation; PEAD replicated internationally but attenuates post-publication, surviving mainly in small, illiquid stocks and largely disappearing among large caps after the mid-2000s in later re-examinations.
openness: No code or data archive (pre-repository era), but the SUE construction and standard CRSP/Compustat inputs are fully specified and have supported many independent reimplementations; the published full text is openly readable via the University of Michigan Deep Blue repository (hdl.handle.net/2027.42/28288).
key_limitation: Tests reuse the same repeatedly consulted 1974-1986 NYSE/AMEX sample in which the hypothesis was generated (Bernard-Thomas 1989), with survivorship from the 1987 CRSP listing requirement and magnitude predictions calibrated to autocorrelations estimated within the same evaluation period.

authors: Tarun Chordia; Amit Goyal; Gil Sadka; Ronnie Sadka; Lakshmanan Shivakumar
title: Liquidity and the Post-Earnings-Announcement Drift
source_tier: peer-reviewed (practitioner journal, tagged separately per protocol)
geography_market: United States: NYSE and Amex common stocks (ADRs, REITs, American trust components, units, closed-end funds, and sub-$5 stocks excluded; average 1,838 stocks)
target: Cross-sectional post-earnings-announcement returns: SUE-decile long-short (earnings momentum) gross and net-of-cost returns and factor alphas
horizon: H3-H4: monthly SUE-decile formation with positions held three months (Jegadeesh-Titman overlapping-portfolio method)
predictor_family: Earnings-surprise events (seasonal-random-walk SUE) conditioned on liquidity (Amihud 2002 illiquidity; Liu 2006 robustness)
model_family: Decile and 10x10 double-sorted portfolios with CAPM/FF3/FF4/FF4+Pastor-Stambaugh alphas; Fama-MacBeth cross-sectional regressions with Shanken correction; net-return accounting under four institutional transaction-cost models
sample_design: All NYSE-Amex common stocks on monthly CRSP and quarterly Compustat, January 1972-December 2005; SUE = most recently announced quarterly earnings minus earnings four quarters prior, scaled by its eight-quarter standard deviation; monthly decile sorts held three months; independent 10x10 SUE-by-Amihud-illiquidity sorts; subperiod split 1972-1988 vs 1989-2005.
benchmark: Zero long-short profit benchmark; CAPM, Fama-French three-factor, four-factor (UMD), and five-factor (UMD + Pastor-Stambaugh traded liquidity) alphas; net returns versus four transaction-cost estimates (Keim-Madhavan 1997, Hanna-Ready 2005, Korajczyk-Sadka 2004, Chen-Stanzl-Watanabe 2004) plus short-lending fees
pit_status: PARTIAL: Largely point-in-time signals: SUE uses the most recently announced quarterly earnings and cross-sectional regressions lag all characteristics two months; however, transaction-cost parameters are fitted ex post on shorter high-frequency subsamples (e.g., KM on 1991-93 institutional trades; spreads from ISSM/TAQ 1988-2005) and extrapolated across the full 1972-2005 window.
native_result: Equal-weighted SUE 10-1 spread is 1.31%/month (FF3 alpha 1.42%, t=9.10); value-weighted only 0.42%. In 10x10 SUE-by-illiquidity sorts the value-weighted long-short earns 0.04%/month in the most liquid decile versus 2.43%/month in the most illiquid (FF3 alpha 2.44%, t=9.06; FF4 2.43%, t=9.69); Fama-MacBeth SUE-x-illiquidity interaction is positive (0.041, t=4.70). Net of transaction costs the most-illiquid spread falls to 1.07% (HR), 0.88% (KM), 0.66% (KS, $1M position), and -0.65% (CSW, $1M); subtracting ~33 bps/month short-borrow cost gives 0.74%, 0.55%, 0.33%, and -0.98% - transaction costs account for 70-100% of the paper profits.
costs_capacity: Costs are the paper's central contribution: four institutional cost models (Keim-Madhavan 1997; Hanna-Ready 2005; Korajczyk-Sadka 2004; Chen-Stanzl-Watanabe 2004), direct ISSM/TAQ effective spreads (round-trip 1.07%/month over the 3-month hold in the most illiquid decile), and ~33 bps/month short-lending fees (Cohen-Diether-Malloy 2007). Capacity is tiny: market impact on a $1 million long-short eliminates ~73% of potential profits (KS) and a $5 million position is unprofitable. Costs declined over time (KM most-illiquid cost 1.73% in 1972-88 vs 1.38% in 1989-2005) but gross drift in illiquid names also fell (2.74% to 2.14%).
replication_decay: PEAD itself is one of the most-replicated anomalies (Ball-Brown 1968; Bernard-Thomas 1989-90), and this study confirms persistence on 1972-2005 data - partly post-discovery - while relocating it to illiquid stocks. Contemporaneous independent spread-based evidence was mixed: Ng-Rusticus-Verdi 2008 found spreads and commissions significantly reduce but do not eliminate PEAD profits, while Battalio-Mendenhall 2007 found the strategy remained profitable after spread costs; Chordia et al. argue both omit the market-impact and short-sale costs their estimates show are decisive. Post-publication evidence (e.g., Martineau, Critical Finance Review 2022) finds PEAD has been absent in large/liquid stocks since about 2006, consistent with the paper's friction-based account of why the drift persisted where it could not be traded.
openness: No public code or data release; inputs are licensed CRSP, Compustat, ISSM, and TAQ. DOI metadata and an SSRN record (abstract 1403342; earlier working paper 972758) are publicly accessible, and the cost-model parameters are taken from published papers (regression coefficients reproduced in the appendix), which aids independent reimplementation.
key_limitation: Full-sample retrospective sorts on a long-mined anomaly with no holdout or forecasting design, and the economic verdict spans profitable to unprofitable depending on the cost model chosen (net most-illiquid spread from +1.07% to -0.98% per month after borrow costs), with cost estimates from short modern high-frequency windows extrapolated back to the 1970s-80s.

authors: Charles Martineau
title: Rest in Peace Post-Earnings Announcement Drift
geography_market: United States individual stocks (NYSE, AMEX, NASDAQ)
target: Post-earnings-announcement buy-and-hold abnormal returns (BHAR[2,60]) conditional on earnings-surprise decile rank
horizon: H3-H4: 2 to 60 trading days after the earnings announcement (about one quarter)
predictor_family: Earnings surprises as event information: analyst-consensus surprises (I/B/E/S median forecast, price-scaled) and seasonal random-walk surprises
model_family: Event-study BHARs by surprise quintile, panel regressions of BHAR[0,1] and BHAR[2,60] on surprise decile ranks with firm and year-quarter fixed effects, and rolling unbiasedness (martingale) regressions
sample_design: U.S. common stocks on NYSE/AMEX/NASDAQ with price above $1 and market cap above $5 million; Compustat sample 1973-2019 (593,654 announcements, random-walk surprises) and I/B/E/S analyst sample 1984-2019 (312,462 announcements); abnormal returns computed against 25 size and book-to-market Fama-French benchmark portfolios; subperiod analysis splits all-but-microcap versus microcap stocks at the NYSE 20th market-cap percentile.
benchmark: Zero post-announcement abnormal return relative to size and book-to-market matched Fama-French benchmark portfolios (no-drift null; announcement-date prices as martingale)
pit_status: PARTIAL: surprise decile breakpoints are formed from prior-quarter observations to avoid look-ahead bias, and day 0 merges the announcement date and the next trading day because precise pre-1996 release timestamps are unavailable (conservative for the day-2+ drift claim); residual caveats are standard I/B/E/S consensus vintage issues and Compustat quarterly EPS for random-walk surprises not stated to be as-first-reported (restatements possible) — both would, if anything, overstate drift, so the adverse conclusion is robust to them.
native_result: PEAD has largely disappeared: analyst-surprise rank no longer significantly predicts BHAR[2,60] after 2005 for all-but-microcap stocks (above the NYSE 20th percentile) and fails in 2016-2019 for microcaps; in the size-quintile analyst-surprise analysis, the only suggestive drift since 2011 is for microcaps at days 2-5 (beta approx. 0.001). Random-walk surprises stopped predicting BHAR[2,60] for all-but-microcap stocks after 1990; microcap random-walk drift persisted longer but since 2016 is confined to days 2-5. Announcement-day incorporation strengthened instead: the BHAR[0,1] response per analyst-surprise decile rose from 20 bps (1984-1990) to 120 bps (2016-2019) for all-but-microcap stocks with R-squared rising from 1.7% to 11.7% (microcaps: 30 to 100 bps, 2.4% to 9.2%), and 2-year rolling unbiasedness-regression slopes for all-but-microcap stocks fell from about 1.6 in 1990 to about 1.0 (prices approx. martingale; downward trend p<0.001) with regression R-squared rising from about 10% to about 25%.
costs_capacity: No trading-strategy cost model; evidence is gross BHAR event-study and regression analysis rather than a long-short portfolio with frictions. The adverse conclusion is cost-robust (costs would only deepen the disappearance); the paper attributes the decay partly to falling trading costs and to high-frequency liquidity providers adjusting quotes to news without trading.
replication_decay: This study is itself the post-publication decay evidence for PEAD, testing the anomaly decades after its 1968-1989 discovery papers; it is consistent with independent monthly-horizon anomaly-attenuation lineages (Chordia-Subrahmanyam-Tong 2014; McLean-Pontiff 2016; Calluzzo-Moneta-Topaloglu 2019) and with Hou-Xue-Zhang (2020) evidence that surviving anomalies concentrate in microcaps; residual short-horizon microcap drift (days 2-5) remains.
openness: Published DOI (10.1561/104.00000122); the published typeset version is freely archived on the Critical Finance Review editor's site (cfr.ivo-welch.org/published/papers/martineau2021rest.pdf); preprint publicly archived on OSF (osf.io/kyqae, single file Draft_v9.pdf — the cited internet appendix is not archived there) and SSRN (abstract 3111607); benchmark portfolios from the public Ken French data library; underlying CRSP/Compustat/I/B/E/S inputs are proprietary but standard; no public replication-code archive identified.
key_limitation: Disappearance is inferred from statistically insignificant coefficients and near-unit unbiasedness slopes rather than formal equivalence tests; pre-1996 announcements lack precise timestamps (day 0 merges two trading days); the analyst-surprise sample requires I/B/E/S coverage, and the residual microcap random-walk drift shows the death of PEAD is scoped to well-covered, larger stocks.

authors: Andrew Ang; Robert J. Hodrick; Yuhang Xing; Xiaoyan Zhang
title: The Cross-Section of Volatility and Expected Returns
geography_market: NYSE, AMEX, and NASDAQ, United States
target: Cross-sectional monthly stock returns
predictor_family: Realized idiosyncratic volatility relative to the Fama-French three-factor model, with aggregate-volatility-risk loadings as companion evidence
model_family: Value-weighted quintile portfolio sorts, double sorts, and CAPM/FF-3 time-series alphas
sample_design: NYSE, AMEX, and NASDAQ stocks, July 1963-December 2000; monthly value-weighted quintile sorts on prior-month daily idiosyncratic volatility (1/0/1 strategy) with double-sort controls; the companion Delta-VIX-loading analysis covers January 1986-December 2000.
benchmark: CAPM and Fama-French three-factor alphas versus the lowest-volatility quintile
pit_status: PIT: idiosyncratic volatility uses prior-month daily CRSP returns and daily FF-3 factors observable at formation; no material accounting-vintage dependence (factor inputs use standard lags), though the daily FF-3 factor series is a retrospective reconstruction.
native_result: Highest idiosyncratic-volatility quintile earns -0.02% per month; the value-weighted 5-1 spread is -1.06% per month (t=-3.10) with FF-3 alpha -1.31% (t=-7.00), surviving size, book-to-market, leverage, liquidity, volume, turnover, bid-ask spread, coskewness, momentum, and analyst-dispersion controls (weakest under dispersion: 5-1 alpha -0.39%, t=-2.09); high Delta-VIX-beta stocks earn a -1.04% monthly 5-1 spread (FF-3 alpha -0.83%) and the estimated price of aggregate volatility risk is about -1% per annum.
costs_capacity: Gross value-weighted portfolio returns only; the highest-volatility quintile averages just 1.9% of market value, so the profitable short leg sits in small, illiquid, costly-to-borrow stocks, and no spread, borrow-fee, turnover, or capacity analysis is provided.
replication_decay: Ang et al. (2009) extend the puzzle to 23 developed markets; Bali and Cakici (2008) show it weakens or vanishes under equal weighting and alternative breakpoints; Fu (2009) and Huang et al. (2010) attribute much of it to one-month return reversal and EGARCH expected volatility; Hou and Loh (2016) find proposed explanations cover under half of the effect.
openness: Verified DOI and journal-typeset full text; inputs are licensed CRSP/Compustat data plus public Fama-French factors and CBOE VXO/VIX; no author code archive, but the sorts are widely reproduced.
key_limitation: Full-sample predictive sorts with no chronological holdout, and the anomalous sign is sensitive in later work to weighting schemes, formation windows, and short-term reversal controls.

authors: Andrea Frazzini; Lasse Heje Pedersen
title: Betting Against Beta
asset_class: Multi-asset: equities, Treasury bonds, corporate credit, and futures/forwards (equity indices, country bonds, FX, commodities)
geography_market: United States (CRSP universe) plus 19 MSCI developed equity markets; U.S. Treasuries and U.S. credit indices; global futures and forwards
target: Cross-sectional risk-adjusted returns: alphas of beta-sorted portfolios and of the long-short beta-neutral betting-against-beta (BAB) factor
horizon: H3: one-month holding period, monthly rebalanced (beta formation windows of 1 year for volatility, 5 years for correlation)
predictor_family: Characteristics and factors: ex-ante market beta estimated from rolling daily returns (1-year volatility, 5-year overlapping 3-day correlations) with Vasicek shrinkage toward 1 (w=0.6)
model_family: Beta-ranked portfolio sorts with rank weighting; low-beta side levered and high-beta side de-levered to ex-ante beta of one; alphas from CAPM and multifactor time-series regressions plus an OLG equilibrium model of leverage constraints
sample_design: U.S. common stocks (CRSP) Jan 1926-Mar 2012; 55,600 stocks in 20 countries, with 19 MSCI developed markets ex-U.S. (Xpressfeed Global) mostly 1989-2012 (Canada 1984); Fama Treasury-bond portfolios (1-10y maturities) 1952-2012; Barclays U.S. credit indices by maturity and rating 1973-2012; AQR internal futures/forwards data 1963-2012. Full-sample retrospective evaluation of monthly-rebalanced long-short BAB factors built from strictly lagged betas; four 20-year subperiods and a DataStream pre-Xpressfeed sample-extension check (Table B7).
benchmark: Zero alpha versus CAPM and Fama-French 3-, Carhart 4-, and Pastor-Stambaugh-augmented 5-factor models for equities; one- or two-factor alphas versus asset-class market portfolios for the non-equity tests (equal-weighted Treasury and credit indices; GDP-weighted equity-index, country-bond, and FX portfolios; equal-risk-weighted commodities)
pit_status: PIT: betas use only lagged market prices and are computable in real time at each monthly rebalance; no macro data-vintage issues. Retrospectively assembled non-equity datasets (Barclays Bond.Hub, AQR internal futures pricing, Credit Suisse distressed index) carry some backfill and coverage risk.
native_result: U.S. equity BAB 1926-Mar 2012: excess return 0.70%/month (t=7.12), CAPM alpha 0.73% (t=7.44), Fama-French 3-factor alpha 0.73% (t=7.39), 4-factor alpha 0.55% (t=5.59), 5-factor alpha 0.55% (t=4.09); annualized Sharpe 0.78 (about twice value, 40% above momentum), significantly positive in each of the four 20-year subperiods. Pooled international BAB alpha 0.28-0.64%/month (t=2.09-4.81); positive Sharpe in 18 of 19 countries and positive 4-factor alpha in 13 of 19, significantly positive in 6 (no negative country alpha significant). U.S. Treasury BAB alpha 0.17%/month (t=6.26), Sharpe 0.81; credit-index BAB 0.11%/month (t=5.14), Sharpe 0.82; rating-sorted credit BAB 0.57%/month (t=3.72). Equity-index, country-bond, FX, and commodity BAB Sharpes 0.11-0.51, individually significant only for equity indices but jointly significant in combination. Higher TED spread is associated with lower contemporaneous BAB returns, and lagged TED predicts BAB negatively.
costs_capacity: No transaction-cost, shorting-fee, financing-spread, or capacity modeling anywhere in the paper; all returns are gross. The factor is levered (long $1.40, short $0.70 per $1 for U.S. equities) with monthly rebalancing of rank-weighted positions that tilt toward small/micro-cap stocks; Novy-Marx and Velikov (2022, JFE) estimate that realistic implementation costs and the embedded equal-weight-like tilts consume most of the equity BAB premium, and leverage financing above T-bills is unmodeled.
replication_decay: Gross low-beta/low-risk effect is one of the most widely reproduced cross-sectional patterns (independent reimplementations across markets and asset classes; AQR posts continuously updated BAB return series). Mechanism and construction are contested post-publication: Bali-Brown-Murray-Tang 2017 attribute it to lottery demand, Schneider-Wagner-Zechner 2020 to skewness, Fama-French 2016 largely subsume it via profitability/investment exposures, and Novy-Marx-Velikov 2022 show the rank-weighting/leveraging scheme drives much of the measured alpha and that net-of-cost performance is far weaker; same-team Asness-Frazzini-Gormsen-Pedersen 2020 defend via betting-against-correlation. Gross premium persists post-2014 but with material net-of-cost decay.
openness: Public DOI and author-hosted full text; AQR's data library publishes updated daily/monthly BAB factor returns for many countries; construction is described in full detail; underlying inputs (CRSP, Compustat/Xpressfeed Global, Barclays Bond.Hub, Credit Suisse distressed index, AQR internal futures pricing) are proprietary and no code is released.
key_limitation: Gross-return evidence: leverage, shorting, financing, and monthly-turnover costs are entirely unmodeled, and the rank-weighted, beta-rescaled construction embeds a micro-cap tilt and relies on noisy ex-ante betas (realized beta of the factor is not zero), so the economic magnitude is sensitive to construction and implementation choices later shown to matter.

authors: Malcolm Baker; Brendan Bradley; Jeffrey Wurgler
title: Benchmarks as Limits to Arbitrage: Understanding the Low-Volatility Anomaly
geography_market: United States individual stocks (full CRSP universe and top 1,000 by market capitalization)
target: Cross-sectional stock and portfolio returns and CAPM alpha of volatility- and beta-sorted quintiles
horizon: H3: one-month holding with monthly rebalance (similar results reported for annual rebalancing)
predictor_family: Risk characteristics: trailing total volatility and trailing market beta
model_family: Cap-weighted quintile portfolio sorts with CAPM regressions; minimum-variance optimization (Clarke-de Silva-Thorley five-factor covariance model)
sample_design: Monthly quintile sorts of all CRSP stocks and the top 1,000 by capitalization on trailing volatility and beta estimated from up to 60 months (minimum 24) of prior returns, January 1968-December 2008; cap-weighted, monthly rebalanced, gross of costs; supplemented by large-cap minimum-variance portfolios with 0-3% weight caps.
benchmark: CRSP value-weighted market return and CAPM security-market line; cross-quintile comparison; information ratios versus the fixed cap-weighted benchmark
pit_status: PIT: sorts use only trailing CRSP return data available at each monthly formation date, and return histories are not subject to revision; no accounting or macro vintages involved.
native_result: $1 in the lowest-volatility quintile of all CRSP stocks in Jan 1968 grew to $59.55 by Dec 2008 versus $0.58 in the highest-volatility quintile (a gain of $10.12 versus a >90% loss in real terms); low-beta $60.46 versus high-beta $3.77. All-stock volatility sorts: Sharpe 0.39 (low) versus -0.05 (high); annualized CAPM alpha +2.08%/yr (t=2.44) versus -8.73%/yr (t=-3.28). Long-only low-volatility information ratios are only 0.08-0.17 versus 0.51 for value and 0.64 for momentum over the same period; a levered large-cap minimum-variance portfolio attains IR 0.45 and alpha 4.70%/yr (t=3.03).
costs_capacity: Headline results exclude all transaction costs; the paper notes monthly-rebalance costs are substantially higher for the high-volatility quintile (so the gross gap understates relative performance) and results are similar with annual rebalancing, but no spread, impact, borrow, or capacity model is estimated; shorting the small-cap high-volatility quintile is flagged as expensive with limited share borrow; the 33% mutual-fund leverage cap and tracking-error mandates are cited as the binding capacity constraint.
replication_decay: The low-risk anomaly has multiple independent lineages before and after this paper (Black 1972; Haugen-Heins 1975; Ang, Hodrick, Xing, Zhang 2006/2009; Blitz-van Vliet 2007; Frazzini-Pedersen betting-against-beta) and international extensions; the paper reports the return gap, if anything, widened after 1983; post-publication work disputes magnitude after profitability and sector controls and warns of crowding/valuation-spread decay as low-volatility products gathered assets after 2011.
openness: Public DOI and publisher metadata; underlying data are commercial CRSP plus Ken French's public data library and Ibbotson series; portfolio calculations were performed at Acadian Asset Management and no code or portfolio-level data were released.
key_limitation: Gross-return retrospective sorts on a single, heavily reused U.S. sample with no formal cost or borrow modeling, and the proposed benchmarking/limits-to-arbitrage mechanism is only indirectly tested; all three authors were consultants to or employees of Acadian Asset Management, a manager of managed-volatility strategies (disclosed).

authors: Robert Novy-Marx; Mihail Velikov
title: Betting against betting against beta
target: Long-short low-beta (BAB) factor returns and net-of-cost alpha
predictor_family: Characteristics and factors (estimated market beta / low-risk)
model_family: Portfolio sorts and factor construction: rank-weighted vs equal- and value-weighted long-short portfolios with beta-scaled hedging; factor-model alpha tests
sample_design: Independent reimplementation of Frazzini-Pedersen (2014) BAB on U.S. CRSP stocks, January 1968-December 2017; replication validated at 98.5% monthly correlation and identical 1.01 Sharpe vs FP's original series over Jan 1968-Mar 2012; construction choices isolated via 'almost BAB' variants and effective-spread transaction-cost accounting.
benchmark: Frazzini-Pedersen BAB as published; standard equal- and value-weighted sorts and directly market-hedged variants; Fama-French five- and six-factor models for (cost-aware generalized) alpha.
pit_status: PIT: signals use only trailing CRSP price data (five-year correlations, one-year volatilities); costs are historical effective spreads; no restated fundamental data involved, so the construction is point-in-time replicable.
native_result: Rank-weighting is a backdoor to equal-weighting: BAB is 99.6% correlated with an equal-weighted-sort version, and per dollar invested BAB commits $1.05 to the bottom 1% of market capitalization (net positions above $1.20 in the bottom 1.7%). Value-weighted BAB earns 56 bp/month (t=3.48) with Sharpe 0.49 vs 1.08 for BAB and an insignificant FF5 alpha of 24 bp/month (t=1.63). Turnover is 214.7%/year (121.1% in the smallest NYSE decile); estimated costs of 60 bp/month cut BAB's profitability by more than 55%, leaving 48 bp/month net (t=3.30) but an insignificant net generalized FF5 alpha of 16 bp/month (t=1.20). FP's beta-compression evidence is a mechanical artifact of their beta estimator: the market's FP-beta averages 1.05 (SD 0.09) with 47% of its variation explained by market volatility.
costs_capacity: Costs are the paper's central contribution: Novy-Marx-Velikov (2016) effective-spread costs and turnover decomposed by NYSE size decile (60 bp/month full sample; 26 bp/month in the last decade), with explicit nano-cap capacity warnings; an 'implementable' rank-and-cap-weighted version costs only 8 bp/month but nets just 43 bp/month (t=2.75) with insignificant generalized alpha. Not modeled: price impact at scale, shorting/borrow fees, and financing spreads on BAB's embedded leverage (157% long / 72% short per dollar).
replication_decay: This study is itself the adverse re-examination lineage for FP (2014) BAB; its mechanical decompositions are arithmetic on public data and no published rebuttal by the original authors was located as of the cutoff. It also documents version drift: AQR's currently maintained BAB series is only 96.2% correlated with, and has a significantly lower Sharpe than, the original paper series. A smaller value-weighted low-beta/defensive premium survives, consistent with the broader contested low-risk literature (lottery-demand and profitability-based explanations).
openness: Public DOI metadata; free author-hosted and SSRN preprints (SSRN 3300965); builds on AQR's publicly posted BAB factor data plus subscription CRSP data; transaction-cost methodology follows the published NV (2016) procedure, later distributed in Velikov's public replication toolkit; no formal journal data/code archive.
key_limitation: A retrospective full-sample decomposition by a single team (with disclosed industry ties) on the same U.S. data as the original; implementability conclusions rest on spread-based cost estimates without market impact or borrow costs, and the critique targets one construction - it does not rule out a smaller value-weighted low-beta premium or settle whether that premium is distinct from profitability/investment exposure.

authors: Amit Goyal; Ivo Welch; Athanasse Zafirov
title: A Comprehensive 2022 Look at the Empirical Performance of Equity Premium Prediction
geography_market: United States aggregate stock market (S&P 500 / CRSP index)
target: Equity premium
horizon: H4: monthly to annual forecast intervals (horizon at least one month)
predictor_family: Valuation, macroeconomic, sentiment, variance, technical, and aggregated cross-sectional predictors
model_family: Univariate OLS predictive regressions with rolling out-of-sample Campbell-Thompson evaluation
sample_design: Replicates 29 predictors from 26 prominent post-2008 papers (at least 100 citations, screened from over a thousand candidates) plus the original 17 Goyal-Welch variables; confirms in-sample results in the authors' own samples (which ended 2000-2017), then extends every series forward to December 2021 (typically about 10 extra years), re-tests in homologous nonoverlapping specifications, and evaluates four simple timing strategies.
benchmark: Expanding historical-mean (prevailing average) equity-premium forecast; all-equity-all-the-time buy-and-hold for investment strategies.
pit_status: PARTIAL — predictors are lagged at native frequencies and 6-month delayed-release variants are checked for the annual variables, but real-time macro vintages (consumption, output gap) are not reconstructed; extended samples embed revised data and include the original discovery periods.
native_result: Of 31 post-2008 predictor series (29 variables plus two July-June annual variants; one semiannual variable, skew, failed replication even in the authors' original sample), 13 have no in-sample predictive ability once data are extended to 2021, and 69% of the 29 variables see t-statistics deteriorate; simulations suggest this joint pattern is more consistent with all 29 having been spurious than with modest stable predictability. In homologous nonoverlapping specifications only 10 variables keep good in-sample performance and only 4 (tchi technical indicators, shtint short interest, accrul aggregate accruals, gpce fourth-quarter PCE growth) also pass rolling OOS-Campbell-Thompson R2. In four simple timing strategies only three annual variables (accrul, gpce, gip) beat all-equity buy-and-hold statistically significantly, each in only one of the four strategies and with weak t-statistics of 1.31, 1.54, and 1.35 (about 16% more strategies outperformed without significance); 84% of variable-based strategies underperform buy-and-hold and about a third of those lose money outright; no variable reliably beats all-equity on gamma-5 certainty-equivalent value.
costs_capacity: No transaction-cost, financing, or capacity modeling; timing strategies are frictionless reallocations between the market index and Treasuries at monthly-to-annual frequency, and CEV results are gross. Because the headline result is adverse, realistic costs would only strengthen it; the authors note OOSCT R2 does not map one-to-one into investment performance.
replication_decay: This is the field's canonical post-publication decay audit rather than a decayed claim itself: roughly 10 post-publication years erase in-sample significance for more than a third of published predictors, consistent with McLean-Pontiff-style decay or original spuriousness; the few survivors are thin (accrul's performance derives exclusively from the dot-com rise and crash around the turn of the millennium; gpce is more consistent).
openness: Open Access (CC BY-NC) at Oxford University Press with an Internet Appendix on the RFS site; Goyal maintains the updated predictor dataset publicly on his website; underlying market series are largely public.
key_limitation: By the authors' own admission not a harsh independent test: extended samples reuse each paper's original discovery period plus only about 10 new years, giving low power against surviving predictors, and the annual survivors rest on few nonoverlapping observations.

authors: Dashan Huang; Jiangyuan Li; Liyao Wang; Guofu Zhou
title: Time series momentum: Is it there?
asset_class: Cross-asset futures and FX forwards (commodities, equity indexes, government bonds, currencies)
geography_market: Fifty-five liquid global instruments: 24 commodity futures, nine developed equity-index futures, 13 developed government-bond futures, nine currency forwards — the Moskowitz-Ooi-Pedersen Table 1 universe (nine underlying currencies rather than the 12 cross-currency pairs MOP trade, hence 55 assets, not 58)
target: Next-month futures/forward excess return; volatility-scaled time-series-momentum strategy returns
horizon: H3; past 12-month return predicting the next month
predictor_family: Own-return time-series momentum/trend (sign and magnitude of the past 12-month return)
model_family: Asset-by-asset and pooled predictive regressions with wild and pairs bootstrap inference and fixed-effects controls; volatility-scaled sign portfolios compared against a no-predictability sign-of-historical-mean strategy
sample_design: Fifty-five liquid futures/forwards, monthly January 1985-December 2015 (extends MOP's 2009 endpoint); asset-by-asset and pooled regressions; recursive out-of-sample evaluation trains on 1985-1999 and evaluates 2000-2015; strategy comparison over the 1986-2015 investment period.
benchmark: Zero-predictability null via parametric wild and nonparametric pairs bootstraps; prevailing-mean forecast (Campbell-Thompson R2_OS); time-series-history (TSH) strategy trading the sign of the expanding historical mean without predictability; Fama-French four-factor and Asness-Moskowitz-Pedersen three-factor adjustments.
pit_status: PIT: predictors are the instruments' own lagged returns and ex ante volatility built from past daily returns; no revised, vintage-sensitive, or look-ahead inputs (the TSH benchmark uses only the expanding mean through month t).
native_result: Asset-by-asset 12m-to-1m regressions: only 8 of 55 slopes significant at 10% (3 at 5%), average in-sample R2 0.39%; recursive 2000-2015 out-of-sample average R2_OS -0.67% with 45 of 55 assets negative and only 3 significant. MOP's pooled t-statistic replicates at 4.34 but is below 5% bootstrap critical values (wild 12.53, pairs 4.83; t falls to 3.37 with fixed effects, below the 3.93 pairs-bootstrap critical value). Equal-weighted TSMOM beats the no-predictability TSH strategy by only 0.14%/month (p=0.19), with FF4 alpha differential 0.10% (p=0.26 in Table 10; the text quotes 0.29); alpha differentials are never significant at the 5% level under any of the four weighting schemes (largest 0.32%/month, p=0.08, under MOP volatility weighting), though raw mean-return gaps reach 0.42%/month (p=0.07) under MOP volatility weighting and 0.45%/month (p=0.03) under the zero-investment scheme. Lewellen predictive slope on TSM forecasts is 0.19 (t=0.61) versus 1 under perfect forecasts.
costs_capacity: No transaction-cost, financing, impact, or capacity modeling; all strategy comparisons are gross. The omission is conservative for the adverse claim, since even gross TSMOM performance is matched by the no-predictability TSH benchmark on the same liquid MOP universe; both strategies' profits stem from their long legs.
replication_decay: Itself the leading independent adverse replication of Moskowitz-Ooi-Pedersen (2012) on the same 55 instruments plus a 2010-2015 extension; corroborates Kim-Tse-Wald (2016) on volatility scaling and Goyal-Jegadeesh (2018) on cross-sectional-versus-time-series decomposition, while century-long multi-market studies (Hurst-Ooi-Pedersen 2017; Georgopoulou-Wang 2017) still report trend profitability, leaving the futures-trend family contested rather than overturned.
openness: Published version paywalled at Elsevier; free public copies via SSRN (abstract 3165284) and the SMU institutional repository (InK); instruments replicate MOP's publicly documented futures/forward universe; an Online Appendix reports robustness; no public code repository.
key_limitation: The paper's own simulations show TSM and TSH strategies are statistically indistinguishable whenever the true pooled slope is small (0.08 in the data; TSM only clearly dominates near 0.4), so failing to reject no-predictability with low-powered asset-level tests cannot rule out a weak but real trend effect — absence of reliable evidence, not evidence of absence.

authors: Brian Hurst; Yao Hua Ooi; Lasse Heje Pedersen
title: A Century of Evidence on Trend-Following Investing
source_tier: practitioner (transparent: data period, construction, costs, fees, and AQR affiliations disclosed; authors' firm sells the strategy)
asset_class: Multi-asset futures and forwards (equity indices, government bonds, currencies, commodities)
geography_market: Global developed markets: 67 markets (11 equity indices, 15 bond markets, 12 currency pairs, 29 commodities)
target: Excess return of a long-short time-series momentum strategy (combined portfolio and per market)
horizon: H3: one-month holding/rebalance from 1-, 3-, and 12-month formation lookbacks (lagged-signal variant also tested)
predictor_family: Momentum, trend, and technical rules: sign of past 1-/3-/12-month excess returns
model_family: Rule-based trading strategy; volatility-targeted long-short positions (10% ex ante portfolio vol), no fitted parameters beyond rolling 3-year volatility/covariance estimates
sample_design: Monthly returns Jan 1880-Dec 2016 across 67 markets; commodity futures 1877-1951 hand-transcribed from Chicago Board of Trade annual reports by two independent vendors and cross-verified; pre-futures assets proxied by cash indexes financed at local short rates; universe at each date limited to markets with data; pre-1985 per-market results presented as out-of-sample relative to Moskowitz-Ooi-Pedersen (2012).
benchmark: Absolute excess return over cash for the self-financing long-short strategy; U.S. 60/40 stock/bond portfolio as the diversification benchmark
pit_status: PARTIAL: signals use only lagged prices, which are point-in-time by construction, but pre-futures-era returns are simulated non-investable proxies (footnote 6 concedes the strategy was not implementable in the 1880s), the 67-market universe reflects retrospective data availability, and cost/fee schedules are retrospective estimates.
native_result: 1880-2016 combined 1/3/12-month time-series momentum at 10% vol target: 18.0% annualized gross excess return, 11.0% net of estimated transaction costs, 7.3% net of costs and 2/20 fees; realized vol 9.7%; net-of-fee-and-cost Sharpe 0.76; full-sample correlation -0.01 to U.S. equities and -0.03 to U.S. 10Y bonds; positive net-of-fee returns in all 14 decade subperiods (weakest 1910-1919: 1.6% net, Sharpe 0.13; the most recent, 2010-2016, has the lowest gross return of any subperiod, 7.6%, with 3.3% net and net Sharpe 0.41); positive gross-of-fee net-of-cost returns in 8 of 10 largest 60/40 drawdowns since 1880; shifting 20% of a 60/40 portfolio into the strategy raises net-of-fee Sharpe from 0.39 to 0.55 and cuts max drawdown from -62.3% to -50.2%; worst strategy drawdown -24.7% (Aug 1947-Feb 1951).
costs_capacity: One-way transaction costs per asset class from AQR's proprietary 2012 estimates (2003-2016: equities 0.06%, bonds 0.01%, commodities 0.10%, currencies 0.03% of notional), doubled for 1993-2002 and sextupled for 1880-1992 following Jones (2002); 2% management plus 20% performance fee with annual high-water mark; futures roll costs excluded and cost estimates acknowledged as significantly uncertain; no capacity or market-impact-at-scale analysis; early-sample instruments were not actually tradable as constructed.
replication_decay: Same-team backward extension of Moskowitz-Ooi-Pedersen (2012), not an independent replication; an earlier AQR white-paper version (Fall 2012) had already examined 1903-June 2012 across 59 markets, so most of the pre-1985 'new' period had been consulted years before journal publication (the 1880-1902 extension and the hand-collected CBOT data first appear in the 2017 version). The paper itself documents recent attenuation: 2010-2016 has the lowest gross return of any subperiod (7.6% vs 18.0% full sample; net-of-fee Sharpe 0.41 vs 0.76; 1-month signal gross Sharpe 0.06 vs 1.38 full sample). Compatible independent long-history evidence exists in the family (Greyserman-Kaminski 2014 spot-based centuries; Georgopoulou-Wang 2017, Review of Finance).
openness: No public code or machine-readable data; hand-collected CBOT commodity series and transaction-cost estimates are AQR-proprietary; remaining inputs are commercial (Bloomberg, Datastream, Global Financial Data, Ibbotson, Citigroup, Morgan Markets); free SSRN version (abstract 2993026) mirrors the article; the rule is simple and fully specified, so approximate reimplementation is feasible on substitute data.
key_limitation: All three authors are principals of AQR, which manages trend-following funds; the same lineage both discovered the rule and assembled the century-long test data, and pre-futures-era returns are simulated non-investable proxies, so the headline net-of-fee Sharpe is a modeled, conflicted backtest rather than auditable third-party evidence.

authors: Linda Canina; Stephen Figlewski
title: The Informational Content of Implied Volatility
geography_market: United States; CBOE S&P 100 (OEX) index options
target: Realized volatility of the S&P 100 index over each option's remaining life
horizon: H3-H4: option's remaining life, from days up to a few months
predictor_family: Options and implied information
model_family: Forecast-efficiency and encompassing OLS regressions with a correction for nonindependent (overlapping cross-section time-series) implied-volatility observations
sample_design: Daily closing prices of S&P 100 (OEX) call options, March 1983 to March 1987 (pre-crash sample, ending before the October 1987 crash), over 17,000 option-price observations; realized volatility measured over each option's remaining life with heavily overlapping windows; regressions run in aggregate and in subsamples split by maturity and strike.
benchmark: Historical volatility estimated from recent index returns (a 60-day window per Christensen and Prabhala's 1998 published account of the CF design); forecast-encompassing comparison
pit_status: PIT: implied volatility is computed from same-day closing option and index prices available at the forecast origin and realized volatility is measured strictly afterward; nonsynchronous option/index closes add measurement error but not lookahead.
native_result: Implied volatility had virtually no correlation with subsequent realized volatility, in aggregate and across subsamples split by maturity and strike (authors' abstract); across CF's reported specifications the slopes in realized-on-implied regressions were roughly 0.14-0.22 (far below the unbiasedness value of 1), and in encompassing regressions the implied-volatility coefficient fell to about 0.04-0.08 and was never significant while historical volatility's coefficient was about 0.50 and significant (CF estimates as quoted by Christensen and Prabhala 1998), so the joint hypothesis that IV is an efficient forecast was strongly rejected.
costs_capacity: Not a trading study: no spread, impact, financing, or capacity analysis; the claim is purely about forecast information content, and any economic use of the finding (e.g., volatility trading against mispriced IV) is untested.
replication_decay: Largely overturned: Christensen and Prabhala (1998, JFE) show that with nonoverlapping monthly sampling over 1983-1995 OEX implied volatility is a biased but informative forecast that outperforms historical volatility and subsumes its information content in some specifications, attributing the CF null to extreme overlap/telescoping in sampling and the low signal-to-noise pre-crash regime; Jorion (1995, currency futures options) and Fleming (1998, OEX) also find implied volatility informative.
openness: No public code or data archive (1993-era study); underlying CBOE OEX closing prices were supplied by Interactive Data Corporation and are commercially, not freely, available; DOI metadata is public and the authors' abstract is posted on the NYU Stern site.
key_limitation: Extreme overlap of consecutive observations (telescoping realized-volatility windows sampled daily) yields imprecise and potentially inconsistent regression estimates, and the sample is confined to the low-volatility pre-crash 1983-1987 regime, which later work shows drives the null result.

authors: Alan Moreira; Tyler Muir
title: Volatility-Managed Portfolios
geography_market: U.S. equity factor portfolios (market, size, value, momentum, profitability, investment, ROE, IA, betting-against-beta) and a multi-currency FX carry factor
target: Risk-adjusted excess returns (alpha, Sharpe ratio, mean-variance utility) of volatility-scaled factor portfolios versus buy-and-hold
horizon: H3: monthly rebalancing; exposure set by previous month's realized variance
predictor_family: Lagged realized variance of the factor's own daily returns (volatility management)
model_family: Deterministic inverse-realized-variance scaling rule; full-sample time-series alpha (spanning) regressions
sample_design: Monthly U.S. factor data: 1926-2015 (Mkt, SMB, HML, Mom), 1963-2015 (RMW, CMA), 1967-2015 (ROE, IA), 1929-2012 (BAB), FX carry 1983-2015; managed factor scales monthly excess return by c over previous-month realized variance from daily data, volatility-matched to buy-and-hold; full-sample regressions plus three 30-year subsample splits.
benchmark: Buy-and-hold original factor with equal unconditional volatility (spanning-regression alpha); Fama-French three-factor controls in robustness
pit_status: PARTIAL: the signal (previous month's realized variance from daily returns) is real-time computable with no parameter estimation, but the volatility-normalization constant c and MVE combination weights are set with full-sample information, evaluation is full-sample, and academic factor returns are retrospectively reconstructed rather than traded series.
native_result: Volatility-managed market factor earns annualized alpha 4.86% (SE 1.56) with beta 0.61 and appraisal ratio 0.34, raising buy-and-hold Sharpe ~25% (0.42 to 0.51); momentum is largest at alpha 12.51% (appraisal 0.875); alphas positive for 9 of 10 factors (SMB -0.58, insignificant); volatility-timed mean-variance-efficient portfolios have appraisal ratios 0.33-0.91; implied mean-variance utility gain ~65% of lifetime utility, versus 35% for expected-return timing in Campbell-Thompson (2008); point estimates positive in all three 30-year subsamples but weak in 1956-1985 (Mkt alpha 2.06, SE 2.82).
costs_capacity: Costs modeled for the market factor only (authors state good cost measures are lacking for other factors): baseline alpha 4.86% gross falls to 3.98% at 10bps and 3.63% at 14bps one-way, break-even 56bps; lower-turnover variants (realized vol, AR(1) expected variance, leverage caps at 1 or 1.5) break even at 74-161bps; ~45-50% utility gains survive no-leverage/50%-margin constraints; options-based embedded leverage yields similar alphas (1986-2012); no market-impact or capacity modeling.
replication_decay: Sharply qualified by independent re-examinations: Cederburg, O'Doherty, Wang, and Yan (JFE 2020, 138(1), 95-117) reproduce the spanning-regression alphas across 103 equity strategies but show the implied trading strategies are not implementable in real time and real-time out-of-sample versions generally earn lower certainty equivalents and Sharpe ratios than the unmanaged portfolios, with the outperforming cases concentrated among momentum-related strategies (consistent with Barroso and Santa-Clara 2015); Barroso and Detzel (JFE 2021, 140(3), 744-767) find volatility management raises turnover up to ~15x and that after transaction costs none of the baseline managed factors earns positive alpha in any sample period, with 6 of 8 having significantly lower net Sharpe ratios, though with cost-mitigation overlays the managed market factor itself stays profitable net of costs, concentrated in easily arbitraged stocks and high-sentiment periods.
openness: Published DOI with public Internet Appendix; inputs are public (Kenneth French library, Hou-Xue-Zhang factors, Frazzini-Pedersen BAB, Lustig-Roussanov-Verdelhan carry data provided by authors); the rule is fully specified and trivially reproducible; no official code archive; authors disclose post-circulation compensated presentations at asset-management firms.
key_limitation: The headline evidence is a full-sample in-sample spanning-regression alpha of a lagged-signal rule — no recursive out-of-sample evaluation — and independent real-time and cost-inclusive replications find the Sharpe/utility gains largely unattainable outside momentum and the cost-mitigated market factor.

authors: Scott Cederburg; Michael S. O'Doherty; Feifei Wang; Xuemin (Sterling) Yan
title: On the Performance of Volatility-Managed Portfolios
geography_market: United States equity factor and long-short anomaly portfolios (CRSP, Compustat, and IBES universe)
target: Real-time Sharpe-ratio and certainty-equivalent gains from volatility-managed versus unmanaged equity strategies
horizon: H3—monthly rebalanced scaling on previous-month realized variance of daily strategy returns
predictor_family: Lagged realized variance as a volatility-management scaling signal
model_family: Inverse-variance volatility scaling, spanning regressions, and real-time mean-variance combination portfolios
sample_design: 103 U.S. equity strategies—the nine Moreira-Muir (2017) factors plus 94 anomaly long-short decile portfolios—with strategy-specific starts from 1926 (market, size, value) to 1986 (latest anomaly) through December 2016; direct Sharpe comparisons, spanning regressions, 100,000-sample bootstrap nulls, and expanding-window real-time combination tests with a 120-month initial training sample, risk aversion of five, a risk-free asset, and a five-times leverage cap.
benchmark: Unmanaged original portfolio plus risk-free asset, with the ex post optimal scaled-unscaled combination as an upper bound
pit_status: PARTIAL—real-time combination tests estimate scaling parameters and portfolio weights only from prior data and lag annual accounting inputs six months, but the direct comparisons and spanning tests use a full-sample scaling constant (scale-invariant metrics mitigate this) and ex post optimal weights that the paper itself shows are unavailable in real time.
native_result: Direct comparisons: volatility-managed versions beat their originals in only 53 of 103 strategies (8 significant at 5%, concentrated in momentum; equal-outperformance null not rejected, binomial p=0.84, while a 100,000-sample bootstrap rejects the persistence-without-risk-return null at p=0.01). In-sample spanning alphas confirm Moreira-Muir (77 of 103 positive, 23 significant; managed-momentum alpha 12.39% per year), but real-time combination strategies earn lower certainty-equivalent returns than the unmanaged original in 72 of 103 cases (market factor: Sharpe 0.42 versus 0.46; CER 1.56% versus 1.75% per year), all 103 fall short of their ex post optimal combinations on CER, no robustness design reverses the result, and Bai-Perron tests find structural breaks in every one of the 103 spanning regressions (mean 2.37 breaks).
costs_capacity: No transaction-cost, turnover, or capacity modeling anywhere in the paper; volatility scaling demands aggressive leverage—the 99th percentile implied position exceeds 400% of capital and reaches 864% for momentum—so the frictionless adverse results if anything understate real-time implementation problems; base-case tests cap absolute risky weights at five and include a risk-free asset.
replication_decay: Independent-team re-evaluation that reproduces Moreira-Muir's (2017) in-sample spanning alphas on extended data while overturning their real-time portfolio implication; consistent with Barroso-Santa-Clara (2015) and Daniel-Moskowitz (2016), gains that survive are concentrated in momentum-related strategies, and later conditional volatility-targeting work recovers benefits only in narrower designs.
openness: Verified Crossref DOI and publisher-typeset PDF publicly hosted by an author; most factor inputs come from the public Ken French and Frazzini data libraries (ROE and IA q-factors were provided by Hou-Xue-Zhang) with anomaly construction documented in the appendix and Internet Appendix, but underlying CRSP/Compustat/IBES data are licensed and no packaged replication code is provided.
key_limitation: The adverse verdict concerns the learnability of ex post combination weights under structural instability, not the existence of volatility predictability itself, and momentum, ROE, and betting-against-beta strategies retain significant real-time gains, so the negative claim covers the general recipe rather than every strategy.
